editorial:
"The Pilgrims" (1924) is a roughly twenty-one-minute silent educational film produced by the Yale University Press Film Service as one of fifteen completed entries in the Chronicles of America Photoplays series. Directed by Edwin L. Hollywood and adapted by William Basil Courtney from Charles M. Andrews's 1919 history "The Fathers of New England," the film dramatizes the Separatists' departure from Scrooby, their years in Leiden, the 1620 Mayflower crossing, and the Plymouth Rock landing — cast members include Robert Gaillard and Harry Simpson, with the Abenaki sagamore Samoset among the figures depicted. Yale registered it on 18 April 1924 with the US Copyright Office under Class LU, registration number LU 20081.

The print is unambiguously public domain: Yale never renewed the copyright, the 28-year statutory term expired in 1952, and the film falls before the 1928 bright line that marks US term expiry. Periscope Film LLC — a stock footage archive — uploaded a transfer to Internet Archive in February 2020 with a CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 tag. A faithful scan of a public-domain print creates no new US copyright under Feist and Bridgeman, so the underlying footage is free. The practical trap for a reuser: if Periscope added a newly composed musical score to that specific transfer, that score is independently protected and the CC license restricts its use. Confirm whether the Internet Archive copy is truly silent before deploying it in any project that will carry an audio track.
faq: Yale University Press produced this — do they still hold the copyright?

No. Yale registered the copyright on 18 April 1924 (Class LU, reg. LU 20081) but never renewed it. The 28-year term under the 1909 Copyright Act expired in 1952, and no renewal entry appears in the Catalog of Copyright Entries for motion pictures covering 1950–1959. Works published in 1924 also crossed the US term-expiry bright line on 1 January 2020.
The Internet Archive copy carries a Creative Commons license — does that restrict how I can use the film?

The CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 on the Periscope Film upload applies only to whatever creative additions Periscope contributed, most plausibly a new musical score or reworked title cards. A mechanical scan of an existing public-domain print generates no new US copyright. The underlying footage is free to use; verify whether that specific transfer includes a newly composed accompaniment before using it in any project that will include the audio track.
